meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Better to remain silent and be thought a fool than to speak and remove all doubt'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Lincoln and not Twain. The earliest known form is Maurice Switzer's 1906 humor book; the Lincoln credit surfaced in 1931.

answer.label: Not Abraham Lincoln — earliest traced to Maurice Switzer (1906)
answer.sourceLine: There is no evidence Lincoln ever said or wrote this. The earliest known version appears in Maurice Switzer’s 1906–1907 humor book “Mrs. Goose, Her Book” — worded “It is better to remain silent at the risk of being thought a fool, than to talk and remove all doubt of it.” The tidy modern wording is a later polish, and the Lincoln credit did not appear until 1931.

source.heading: The source
source.excerpt: It is better to remain silent at the risk of being thought a fool, than to talk and remove all doubt of it.
trail: Quote Investigator traces the earliest known version to Maurice Switzer’s 1906–1907 book “Mrs. Goose, Her Book” and finds “no substantive evidence that either Abraham Lincoln or Mark Twain employed this maxim” (quoteinvestigator.com ↗).
The earliest Lincoln attribution QI found appeared in Golden Book Magazine in November 1931 — 66 years after Lincoln’s death (quoteinvestigator.com ↗).
Switzer’s book survives in full — the copyright-1906 original is digitized at the Internet Archive ↗, catalogued under “Switzer, Maurice, b. 1870.”
The idea echoes an ancient proverb — Proverbs 17:28: “Even a fool, when he holdeth his peace, is counted wise” — but the modern epigram is not a Bible quotation.
source.excerptNote: The wording in Switzer’s 1906 book — the earliest known appearance. The familiar “…be thought a fool than to speak and remove all doubt” is a later, smoother paraphrase whose exact source is unknown.
source.rightsNote: Switzer’s 1906–1907 book “Mrs. Goose, Her Book” is itself in the public domain in the U.S. (published before 1931), but its wording differs from the line shown here. The exact popular phrasing is an unattributed modern paraphrase with no identifiable first publication, so its rights status cannot be asserted.

author.name: Maurice Switzer
author.heading: About Maurice Switzer
author.bio: Maurice Switzer (born 1870) was an American humorist and advertising man whose 1906 collection Mrs. Goose, Her Book mixed nonsense verse with satirical quips for adults. It contains the earliest known version of this maxim, though Switzer himself was riffing on a much older proverbial idea. He is the leading candidate for the saying’s origin — not its certain author, and certainly not the smoother modern wording.

misattribution.heading: How Lincoln got the credit
misattribution.intro: This is one of the internet’s classic “wise old figure” misattributions — pinned on Lincoln and Twain because both are magnets for pithy wisdom. Neither has any documented connection to it.

items.why: Lincoln died in 1865; the earliest attribution to him that Quote Investigator located is from Golden Book Magazine, November 1931 — 66 years later, with no source (quoteinvestigator.com ↗).
Twain connections surfaced even later (around 1953). Ken Burns’s 2001 Twain documentary companion book listed this line under “What Twain Didn’t Say” (quoteinvestigator.com ↗).
Often tagged “Confucius” or quoted as scripture. The nearest real ancestor is Proverbs 17:28, but the modern epigram is not a quotation from either.

misattribution.truthLine: The earliest known version is Maurice Switzer’s, in his 1906 book Mrs. Goose, Her Book — and even he worded it differently from the line we quote today (quoteinvestigator.com ↗).

context.heading: Why the misattribution sticks
lead: The saying rewards its speaker with an air of shrewd modesty, so it drifts naturally toward the era’s most quotable sages. Lincoln and Twain are the default hosts for any homespun American wit whose real author has been forgotten — a phenomenon Twain scholars and Lincoln archivists both wearily document.

The line also has a genuinely old pedigree in idea, if not in wording: Proverbs 17:28 makes the same point millennia earlier. That deep familiarity makes the modern epigram feel ancient and authorless, which is exactly the vacuum a big name rushes to fill.
context.pull: Not Lincoln, not Twain — earliest traced to a 1906 humor book.
